title: ACID, savepoints, MVCC: why readers don't block writers
summary: A transaction is all or nothing, and one failed statement aborts all of it unless a savepoint contains the damage. Postgres isolates transactions with row versions instead of read locks, so readers and writers never wait for each other; only two writers on the same row do.

examples.title: UPDATE writes a new row version; ROLLBACK TO just hides it

annotations.note: Transaction IDs change on every run, so xmin is compared, not printed. pg_current_xact_id() (PostgreSQL 13+) returns the 64-bit xid8; the cast gives the 32-bit form that xmin uses. Both rows were written by this script's one transaction, and xmax 0 means no transaction has deleted or replaced them.

Row a moved from (0,1) to (0,3): 60 is a new version. The 100 is still on the page, its xmax set to our transaction. We no longer see it, but a concurrent transaction would, until we commit. That old version is what lets readers proceed without waiting for writers.

SAVEPOINT starts a subtransaction. Its update gets a transaction ID of its own and writes version (0,4). ROLLBACK TO marks that subtransaction aborted, releases the locks taken since the savepoint, and leaves the outer transaction usable.

The docs say a nonzero xmax on a visible row usually means the deleting transaction hasn't committed yet, or that an attempted deletion was rolled back. Here it's the second case: rolling back did not restore the old version, it only marked the newer one's writer as aborted, so visibility checks skip it.
The aborted version still occupies slot 4, so the new version lands in slot 5. Versions from rolled-back work are garbage that VACUUM collects later (the last lesson of this module).

examples.title: Two sessions: the reader doesn't wait, the second writer does
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE accounts (id text PRIMARY KEY, balance int NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('a', 100), ('b', 0);

annotations.note: A has written new versions of both rows and holds a row lock on each until it ends. Nothing is visible to other sessions yet.

B never ran BEGIN, so each of its statements is its own transaction. Its snapshot shows the last committed versions, 100 and 0: no waiting, and never the in-between state where the 40 has left a but not reached b.

How the runner shows a wait: a step still running after 400 ms is printed as "[5] B: waiting" and the script moves on, as you would switch terminals; the result is printed under the same number when it arrives. B needs the row lock A holds on a, so it waits for A's commit or rollback.

A's COMMIT releases the locks and B's update completes right after it. Under READ COMMITTED a blocked UPDATE re-reads the row once the other transaction commits, so it adds 1 to A's 60, not to the 100 it saw when it started. Nothing was lost: 61 and 40.

examples.title: One error aborts the transaction; a savepoint contains it
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE accounts (id text PRIMARY KEY, balance int NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('a', 100), ('b', 0);

annotations.note: The duplicate key fails (23505), and from then on the whole transaction is aborted: every statement is refused with 25P02 until it ends. The successful insert of c is doomed too.

COMMIT on an aborted transaction doesn't raise an error. It rolls back and reports the command tag ROLLBACK. pgx turns that tag into pgx.ErrTxCommitRollback; code that ignores Commit's error believes it saved data that is gone.
With a savepoint in front of the risky statement, ROLLBACK TO undoes just that statement and clears the aborted state. The insert of c, made before the savepoint, survives.
A second connection sees c and d from the committed transaction and nothing from the failed one: all or nothing, and once COMMIT returned, durable.

use_cases: Any change that spans several statements and must happen completely or not at all: a transfer, an order with its lines, a schema migration
Imports that should skip bad rows instead of failing: a savepoint around the risky statement, ROLLBACK TO on error, carry on
Long reads (exports, reports) next to normal write traffic, without either side waiting for the other
strengths: Plain reads take no row locks: a long report never stalls updates, unlike a Java ReentrantReadWriteLock, where one writer waits for every reader to finish
ROLLBACK doesn't copy old values back; it marks the transaction aborted and visibility checks skip what it wrote
Most DDL is transactional too: a migration's CREATE, ALTER and data fixes commit or roll back together
Savepoints give statement-level recovery inside a transaction; PL/pgSQL's EXCEPTION blocks use the same subtransaction mechanism
weaknesses: Every UPDATE writes a whole new row version, usually with new index entries, so update-heavy tables grow until VACUUM reclaims the old versions
Any error aborts the entire transaction; recovering needs a savepoint, which costs a subtransaction
MVCC removes read/write blocking, not write/write blocking: writers to the same row still queue
Under the default READ COMMITTED each statement takes a fresh snapshot, so two reads in one transaction can disagree (next lesson)

pitfalls.title: Ignoring Commit's error
pitfalls.detail: COMMIT of an aborted transaction succeeds as a statement and reports ROLLBACK. pgx returns pgx.ErrTxCommitRollback for it, so the error from tx.Commit is the only signal that your writes are gone.

pitfalls.title: Catching an error and carrying on in the same transaction
pitfalls.detail: After any error every statement fails with 25P02 until ROLLBACK. If you expect a statement to fail (a duplicate during an import), put a savepoint in front of it, or better, write it so it can't fail.
pitfalls.bad: INSERT INTO tags VALUES ('go');  -- may be a duplicate: aborts the transaction
pitfalls.good: INSERT INTO tags VALUES ('go') ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

pitfalls.title: A savepoint per row in a big loop
pitfalls.detail: Each savepoint is a subtransaction. The docs warn that overhead grows with the number kept open, and past 64 per backend lookups go to pg_subtrans on disk. Release savepoints you no longer need, and prefer ON CONFLICT or a staging table to a savepoint per row.

pitfalls.title: Leaving a transaction open
pitfalls.detail: An idle transaction keeps its row locks and stops VACUUM from removing versions it might still see. Never wait for user input, an HTTP call or a slow job inside a transaction; idle_in_transaction_session_timeout is the server-side safety net.

quiz.q: Session A has updated row a but not committed. Session B runs SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 'a'. What happens?
options: B waits until A commits or rolls back
B immediately gets the last committed value
quiz.why: B's snapshot doesn't include A's uncommitted version, and plain reads take no row locks, so it reads the previous version without waiting.

quiz.q: Inside a transaction an INSERT fails with a unique violation. What does the next SELECT do?
options: Runs normally: only the INSERT was undone
Fails with 25P02 until the transaction ends
quiz.why: Postgres aborts the whole transaction on an error. Only ROLLBACK (or ROLLBACK TO a savepoint taken before the error) makes it usable again.

quiz.q: What does ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s do?
options: Undoes the work done after s and leaves the transaction open
Undoes the work done before s
quiz.why: The savepoint's subtransaction is aborted; everything before it is kept, and the transaction can continue and commit.

quiz.q: UPDATE accounts SET balance = 60 WHERE id = 'a' has committed. What happened on disk?
options: The row was overwritten in place
A new row version was written; the old one stays until VACUUM removes it once no snapshot can see it
The old version was moved to an undo log
quiz.why: Every update creates a new version with a new ctid. The old one is dead but stays in the table until VACUUM, which is what keeps it available to older snapshots.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: System Columns (xmin, xmax, ctid)
PostgreSQL docs: Asynchronous Commit (what COMMIT normally guarantees)

body:
## Concept

A transaction is the unit of correctness. Everything between `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` is:

- **Atomic**: all of it takes effect or none of it does. In Postgres a single failed
  statement aborts the whole transaction; a **savepoint** lets you roll back to a point
  inside it and continue.
- **Consistent**: constraints are checked, so a committed state never violates them.
- **Isolated**: other sessions don't see your changes until you commit, and you don't
  see theirs half-done.
- **Durable**: by default `COMMIT` returns only after the transaction's WAL records are
  flushed to disk, so a reported commit survives a crash.

Postgres isolates with **MVCC** (multiversion concurrency control). An `UPDATE` never
changes a row in place: it writes a new **row version** and marks the old one as replaced.
Each statement reads from a **snapshot** that decides which versions it may see. A reader
therefore never needs a writer's lock: it takes the newest version its snapshot allows.
Only two writers on the same row wait for each other.

Examples 2 and 3 use the two-session runner: steps tagged `A:` and `B:` run on two
connections, in script order, like two psql terminals side by side.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java/C++ locks:** a `ReadWriteLock` makes writers wait for readers. MVCC works like
  copy-on-write: a writer publishes a new version and readers keep the one they started
  with. In Go terms, it's closer to swapping an `atomic.Pointer` to an immutable struct
  than to a `sync.RWMutex`.
- **Python (psycopg) and Go (pgx):** the "poisoned transaction" is the classic surprise.
  psycopg raises `InFailedSqlTransaction` on the next statement after an error; that is
  SQLSTATE 25P02 from example 3. In pgx, check the error from `tx.Commit`.
- **Connection pools (pgxpool, node-postgres):** a transaction lives on one connection.
  Sending `BEGIN` through the pool and then another statement through the pool may use
  two different connections. Use the pool's transaction API (`pool.Begin` in pgx), which
  pins one connection until `Commit` or `Rollback`.
- **C:** think of `xmin` and `xmax` as a version stamp in every record header: "written by
  transaction X, superseded by transaction Y".

## How it works

Every row version carries the hidden columns from example 1: `xmin` (the transaction that
wrote it), `xmax` (the transaction that deleted or replaced it, or 0) and `ctid` (its
physical place, page and slot). Postgres also records for each transaction whether it
committed or aborted. Roughly, a version is visible to your snapshot if its `xmin`
committed before the snapshot was taken (or is your own transaction), and its `xmax` is
0, aborted, or not yet committed as far as the snapshot knows.

That is why `ROLLBACK` is cheap: it records "aborted" and every version the transaction
wrote becomes invisible. The cost comes later: dead versions stay in the table until
`VACUUM` removes the ones no snapshot can still see (lesson 7).

The `sql` runtime of example 1 runs your script inside one transaction that is always
rolled back, so it can show savepoints but not `COMMIT`; the two-session examples commit
for real, in a throwaway schema.

## Design notes

- **Keep transactions short.** Row locks are held until the end, and an open transaction
  holds back VACUUM. Do the HTTP call, the file upload or the user prompt before `BEGIN`
  or after `COMMIT`, never in between.
- **One place owns the boundary.** In Go, a small `WithTx(ctx, func(pgx.Tx) error)`
  helper begins, rolls back on error, and commits (the Go + PostgreSQL module builds it).
  Repositories take a `pgx.Tx` (or an interface it satisfies) instead of beginning
  their own.
- **Prefer statements that can't fail over savepoints.** `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, `WHERE
  NOT EXISTS`, or a staging table is cheaper and clearer than catching duplicates.
  Savepoints are for genuinely unpredictable failures inside a larger unit of work.
- MVCC only removes read/write blocking. When two transactions write the same rows, you
  still choose how they coordinate: isolation levels (next two lessons) or explicit row
  locks (lesson 4).

INSERT 0 2
SELECT 2
    id | balance | ctid  | written_by_me | xmax
    ---+---------+-------+---------------+-----
    a  | 100     | (0,1) | t             | 0
    b  | 0       | (0,2) | t             | 0
UPDATE 1
SELECT 2
    id | balance | ctid  | xmax
    ---+---------+-------+-----
    a  | 60      | (0,3) | 0
    b  | 0       | (0,2) | 0
SAVEPOINT
UPDATE 1
SELECT 1
    id | balance | ctid
    ---+---------+------
    a  | 55      | (0,4)
ROLLBACK
SELECT 1
    id | balance | ctid  | xmax_set
    ---+---------+-------+---------
    a  | 60      | (0,3) | t
UPDATE 1
    id | balance | ctid
    ---+---------+------
    a  | 59      | (0,5)
